body.text: The wafer-thin 5:4 majority ruling by a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court calling for the revision of the term “industry” has drawn the ire of trade unions and Left parties.

The Bench ruled that the expansive definition of industry, based on the “triple test” standard laid down in a 1978 seven-judge Bench judgment, needed revisitation and that the nature of the activity would determine what constitutes an industry, not merely the presence or existence of employer-employee relations. This, unions say, will impact the working classes by excluding many types of work from the purview of industrial relations and expose them to a wide range of vulnerabilities. Four judges opined that the definition did not warrant a revisitation.

Section 2(j) of the now repealed (on February 2, 2026) Industrial Disputes Act defines industry as “any business, trade, undertaking, manufacture, calling of employers and includes any calling, service or employment, handicraft, or industrial occupation or avocation of workmen”. The scope of this definition has been the subject of judicial scrutiny over the years. The definition was further expanded in a 1978 majority ruling of the Supreme Court (Bangalore Water Supply & Sewage Board vs. A. Rajappa & Others); that definition “held the field” for almost half a century.
It is that order and its re-formulated definition of industry that the nine-judge Bench has sought to correct.

Employees of the Bengaluru Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB) were penalised for alleged misconduct, and they went to the Labour Court against this move. The BWSSB argued that because it provided basic civic amenities to the public, it could not be called an industry under Section 2(j) of the ID Act. It contended that it fell outside the ambit of the Act and the Labour Court had no jurisdiction over it. The logic was simple: if the BWSSB was not an industry, its employees could not claim the status of “workmen”. The matter went to the Karnataka High Court and then to the Supreme Court.

A majority of five judges (on a seven-judge Bench), in a judgment authored by Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, arrived at an expansive term of industry, adopting what came to be known as the “triple test”.

The “triple test” required a systematic and organised activity; cooperation between employer and employee in the conduct of such activity; and the production of goods and services directed towards the satisfaction of human wants and wishes. The idea was to cover a wide spectrum of economic and quasi-economic undertakings. An enterprise would fall within the ambit of industry irrespective of whether it was in the private, joint, or public sector. What was material was how it was organised and not the nature of its activity. The triple test formulation was accepted by all seven judges; the only area of divergence was regarding the manner and extent of its application.

It was also agreed that the interpretive exercise must remain faithful to the statutory objective, which was promotion of industrial peace and orderly regulation and resolution of disputes between employers and workmen. It was also agreed that the definition would not apply to a limited category of institutions where minimal or marginal engagement of labour was in force. Therefore, eleemosynary and altruistic institutions did not fall in the definitional ambit of industry.

The judgment also included the “dominant nature test”, which basically meant that if the dominant nature of the activity in the undertaking satisfied the criteria of “industry”, then it would be classified as one even if certain components or individuals did not satisfy that condition. Exemptions could be made for “sovereign” functions but they must be narrowly construed.

Therefore, welfare activities undertaken by the state would be covered by the definition of industry. Services, as long as they formed a part of the wealth of the nation, such as educational services, were industrial in nature. Units within departments discharging sovereign functions could fall within Section 2(j) of the IDA. Finally, the legislature had the ultimate authority to exclude activities from the operation of the Act.

The nine-judge Bench judgment reformulated the principles of the “triple test” in the BWSSB case. The Bench, however, said that the “triple test” would apply to proceedings that are pending. The “reformulated” triple test will apply prospectively.

It was also clarified that the seven-judge Bench order would no longer be regarded as the “sheet anchor for the interpretation of the IR Code [the new Industrial Relations Code] or any of its provisions, should such a question arise in the future”. Also, any issue arising from the IR Code would not be influenced by the reformulated “triple test”. Trade unions are of the opinion that such remarks were unnecessary as it appeared as if the Bench had given a carte blanche to the IR Code.
The justification

Indeed, there have been recurring judicial calls for a reconsideration of the Krishna Iyer-authored judgment and the definition of industry under the ID Act. In 1982, Parliament amended the IDA; the amendment was passed in 1984. It retained the core of the “triple test” but introduced certain exceptions. But the amended portions were never notified. Despite the divergence of opinions over the years, the seven-judge Bench decision in the BWSSB case prevailed. One of the core principles of the reformulated definition was that an activity undertaken by the state would not automatically entitle it to the “sovereign functions” exception.

In 2001, the BWSSB judgment was referred for reconsideration by a larger Bench following a divergence of decisions between two separate judgments. One had an expansive interpretation; the other, a restrictive one. On January 2, 2017, a seven-judge Bench directed that a nine-judge Bench be constituted to hear the matter. On September 12, 2023, the matter was listed for a final hearing. Meanwhile, the IR Code came into force on November 21, 2025. On February 2, 2026, the ID Act was repealed. The IR Code had further whittled down the definition of industry.

On February 2, 2026, in order to settle the controversy, the court, via an order, framed the following questions for seeking a final resolution: whether the “triple test” was correct law; whether the IDA or the IR Code had any legal impact on the interpretation of industry as laid down in the principal Act; whether social welfare activities or schemes of government departments could be classified as industry under Section 2(j); and what were the sovereign functions of the state that fell outside the purview of the section. The matter was heard on March 17, 18, and 19 this year.
The new definition

Some of the issues before the nine-judge Bench were: how was the definition of industry as given in Section 2(j) of the IDA to be understood and applied, be it in an expansive or a restricted sense; whether an organisation was to be viewed as one whole or its constituent units viewed in isolation; whether welfare and public institutions fell within the ambit of industry and the extent to which the “sovereign function” exception could operate in order to exclude certain activities from its reach.

An industry would now be defined as one where systematic activity took place and such activity was organised through cooperation between employer and employee. In the case of production, distribution, and provision of services possessing a discernible commercial character that was analogous to trade or business and calculated to satisfy material wants and wishes (distinguishable from activities that were purely spiritual or religious in nature, though not excluding the provision of material goods and services merely because they are associated with a religious objective) a prima facie assumption shall arise that the undertaking constituted an industry under Section 2(j). The profit motive was irrelevant; the decisive test was the nature of the activity and employer-employee relations.

While the five judges of the majority opinion, including Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, upheld the need for reformulating the “triple test” formula, Justice B.V. Nagarathna and three others held that a reconsideration of the 1978 judgment was not warranted. The “triple test” was “good law”, Justice Nagarathna averred in her dissent. The new law (IR Code) with its new definition of industry should not be a reason to reconsider the judgment of this court in the BWSSB case, she held.

The IR Code, which most central trade unions have opposed in toto, purportedly removes interpretational ambiguities in its definition of industry. It provides an exception to the sovereign functions of the appropriate government. It also allows the Central government to notify additional activities that can be excluded from the ambit of industry and “regulation”.

The 1978 ruling in the BWSSB case provided workers with a means to address their grievances relating to their conditions of employment. With the government opening up its sectors to the private sector, the need for an expansive definition of industry was warranted. It offered the possibility of justice to all categories of employees, even those who were not covered by specific statutes, Justice Nagarathna said.
Warp and weft of labour law

Justice Nagarathna opined that the 1978 judgment had become the foundation on which both public and private sectors had structured their conduct for about five decades. The judgment was cited in at least 84 Supreme Court cases, of which 31 followed it in labour disputes, 20 followed it in the context of principles of statutory interpretation, 10 “distinguished it on facts”,18 referred to it in varying contexts, and only 5 doubted its correctness. It was woven in the warp and weft of labour law, she held. To disturb it would neither advance the law nor serve any prospective purpose. It would reopen settled questions that even the Legislature had left behind.

She referred to how activities earlier undertaken by the Central or State governments were privatised, and private players, either by themselves or through a private-public arrangement, were carrying out developmental and welfare projects and programmes. These activities by private parties would employ workmen and employees whose interests would have to be protected under the ID Act by giving meaning to the word “industry” as laid down in the “triple test”, she held.

The BWSSB judgment could be watered down to the detriment of employees and workmen. A narrowly tailored definition of industry would not assist in maintaining industrial peace, protection of workmen and employers envisaged under the scheme of the ID Act. With the gradual delicensing of several industries, the decision of the seven-judge Bench was more relevant in the present scenario, she stated in her dissenting opinion.

Explaining why an expansive definition of industry was necessary, she held that along with increased worker vulnerability due to privatisation and the resulting lack of statutory service rules, the pressure to reduce costs could result in companies “structuring” themselves outside the purview of industry, thus finding a way to escape regulatory laws and associated labour costs. This amplified the need for an expansive definition of industry.

Certain activities, like the production of goods and services, undertaken by the state were being done by private entities, either individuals or corporates. She cautioned that changes in the economy, economic thinking, and the drastic consequences of these in the last 35 years needed to be borne in mind. The definition of industry, under Section 2(j) of the ID Act, cannot be curtailed or given a restricted meaning, given the privatisation of industries and the transfer of many social welfare activities of the state into private hands and entities. The ID Act was very much relevant, she held, for considering cases pending before tribunals and courts concerning employers and workmen.

She went a step further to state that the “liberalisation privatisation globalisation” model had favoured one stakeholder in the tripartite stakeholder model under the ID Act, namely, the employers in the private sector. Employers now possessed a supercharged version of bargaining power which was earlier kept in check. But now, with employers holding greater bargaining power, market forces, along with concomitant pressures on the state to ensure economic growth and development, augmented worker vulnerability. An expansive definition of industry serves the purpose of acting as a mitigating force and a bulwark against this skewed bargaining power, especially turning exploitative, by allowing for the state to not completely abdicate its obligations as a stakeholder to intervene, when necessary, she stated in her dissenting opinion.

Unions are legitimately angry over the Supreme Court ruling. In a statement, the Centre of Indian Trade Unions held that the four new labour codes, including the IR Code, had excluded millions of workers from protection by increasing the threshold for the application of existing laws. The judgment had in a way facilitated the interests of corporates.

Elamaram Kareem, former MP and general secretary of the Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU), told Frontline that the Supreme Court had let down Indian workers. In 1978, Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer had delivered a landmark judgment in the BWSSB case that provided a safeguard for working people by giving an expansive definition of “industry”, he said.

The judgment had laid down the “triple test” for determining what constituted an industry, which had stood the test of time. “Now the nine-judge Bench says that definition is not applicable to the IR Code,” Kareem said. The 1978 judgment had also held that profit motive could not be the sole criterion for determining whether an institution was an industry.

Kareem pointed to private hospitals and educational institutions that operate for profit, as well as the Tirupati Devaswom, which employs more than 20,000 workers. Spiritual activity could be exempt from the definition of industrial activity, he said, but manufacturing laddoos, cleaning premises and other such work was no different from ordinary industrial work. Workers engaged in these activities would be affected by the verdict. “We strongly oppose the spirit of the verdict,” Kareem said, adding that CITU was planning appropriate action. He called it unfortunate that a judicial verdict had upheld the IR Code. “The judiciary was the only forum we expected justice from,” he said.

Amarjit Kaur, general secretary of the All India Trade Union Congress, agreed. Trade unions had long fought for a comprehensive definition of “industry”, she said, while the definition laid down by Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer had repeatedly been challenged in court. “Those in government today had never wanted this definition of industry,” Kaur said. Their aim, she argued, was to exclude as many people as possible from the definition of “worker”.

During the proceedings, the government counsel had argued that the court need not pronounce a judgment and could leave the definition of industry to the government. “The implications of this judgment are grave,” Kaur said. If the government, as the model employer, decided that hospitals, schools and universities did not fall within the definition of industry, their employees would be outside the protection of labour laws and collective bargaining.

She also warned that the government could deregister trade unions or cancel their registration. “The IR Code allows the government to have sovereign rights over anything,” she said. Organised-sector unions, which still had considerable influence, were now the government’s target, she argued.

Kaur said the judgment would strengthen the ideology underlying the labour codes and the draft labour policy. “These are different ways of killing the Constitution,” she said. The AITUC would challenge the judgment and was already consulting lawyers. She also pointed out that the judgment had been decided by a “wafer-thin majority”.

With precarity of employment becoming the norm and the government being inclined to move towards “ease of doing business” favouring industry, it is feared that the actual producers of wealth will be eased out of the ambit of protective labour laws if the Supreme Court judgment actually comes into effect.

While referring to the litigation and judicial to-and-fro in the matter, the Bench observed that it was like the proverbial “albatross around the mariner’s neck”. Only time will tell around whose hapless neck the reworked triple test or the labour codes is destined to hand like the albatross.
